About me

I am a Ph.D. student in Electrical and Computer Engineering at The University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP), where I started in Fall 2025, and a research associate at the Edge and BioMedical Intelligence Lab. My research focuses on efficient AI, hardware–software co-design for efficient AI acceleration, and leveraging LLMs for chip design, covering both AI for hardware and hardware for AI.

Over the past year, I have gained experience in each of these fields. So far, I have two published works, one journal paper in submission, and two projects in progress.

I received my B.Sc. in Electrical and Electronic Engineering from Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET). My research journey began with my undergraduate thesis, where I proposed a lightweight deep neural network for MRI image segmentation.

I love solving math, through all its ups and downs. That love has been the main drive behind all the work I have done so far, and behind the work I look forward to doing. In my free time, I like to watch reels, play badminton, try new tunes on the ukulele, and travel.

In submission

ReSPLIN: energy-efficient long-context pruning for LLMs

Most pruning methods make weights zero but still run the full dense multiply, so the GPU does the same work. ReSPLIN changes the modules themselves, so the savings show up on the power meter.

Approach

Calibration-only and static: a small calibration set identifies important MLP channels and attention projections, then a fixed compressed model is built before deployment. Selected MLP channels are physically removed and some attention projections become low-rank modules. No retraining, fine-tuning, masking, or dynamic routing.

Result

Compared with the dense baseline and five other pruning and compression methods across context lengths from 512 to 16,384 tokens, it was the only one to reduce energy per token and increase throughput at every length, while matching FLAP's perplexity recovery and beating LLM-Pruner.

  • Lower energy / tokenat every context length tested
  • Higher throughputthan dense at every length
  • 0 retrainingpost-training, calibration only
Code and full results on GitHub
Completed, Ph.D. project

EdgeSWA: sliding-window attention accelerator on PYNQ-Z1

Full self-attention grows quadratically with sequence length, which a small FPGA can't afford. EdgeSWA computes only a local window per token and approximates the expensive parts of SoftMax, then runs on a physical board.

Approach

Fixed-point HLS accelerator with an input-stationary dataflow that keeps each query on-chip while keys and values stream through. Piecewise approximations replace SoftMax's exponential and division. The ARM core controls it over AXI-Lite; tensors move over AXI HP from DDR. Built with Vitis HLS and Vivado 2025.2.

Result

On a physical PYNQ-Z1, attention for 128 tokens takes 1.3 ms in hardware versus 788 ms on the board's ARM CPU, a 602× speedup. 98.3% of outputs match the software reference, the design meets timing at 100 MHz, and it uses at most 17% of any FPGA resource.

  • 602× fasterthan the ARM CPU at N = 128
  • 1.31 mshardware latency at N = 128
  • 98.3% matchwith the software reference
  • 17% LUTstiming met at 100 MHz

Accepted, IEEE EMBC 2026

Parameter-efficient Conv-GRU for personalized insulin and meal recommendations

People with Type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections have few personalized tools for deciding insulin and carbohydrate doses. This model recommends both, for a glucose target 30 to 90 minutes after a meal, and is small enough for a wearable.

Approach

A Conv-GRU with temporal masking as regularization to curb overfitting to time patterns, pretrained across subjects and fine-tuned per person, predicting at 5-minute steps.

Result

Lower RMSE and MAE than heuristic baselines, Chained-LSTM, and N-BEATS on the OhioT1DM dataset across insulin and carbohydrate scenarios, with a fraction of their parameters.

  • ≈80 kBtotal memory footprint
  • 31.5% fewerparameters than Chained-LSTM
  • >90.5% fewerparameters than N-BEATS

Accepted, IEEE MWSCAS 2026

Embedded AI for Subject-Independent Brain Computer Interface using EEG Signals

Ivan Meraz, Matthew Amezaga, Md Rifatul Islam, Fariza Siddiqua, Md Maruf Hossain Shuvo

Motor-imagery brain–computer interfaces usually need dense electrode caps and 20–40 minutes of calibration for each new user. This system decodes four imagined movements from just four EEG channels on a consumer headset, with no calibration, and runs on an edge device.

Approach

MSAENet4Ch, a compact network built on EEGNet that shifts capacity to time: four parallel temporal convolutions (100–800 ms windows), squeeze-and-excitation channel attention, temporal attention pooling, and a gradient-reversal branch that removes subject identity during training. Euclidean alignment from a 30-second resting recording adapts to each user without labels. Live pipeline: OpenBCI Ganglion, MATLAB filtering, Jetson Orin Nano inference, ESP32-S3 Bluetooth mouse.

Result

Trained on the PhysioNet motor-imagery dataset (109 subjects, split by subject) and tested on 16 people the model never saw, it reaches 43.22% four-class accuracy against 25% chance, 4.56 points above EEGNet, with zero labeled calibration trials. 14 of the 16 test subjects scored above chance. Inference takes 0.75 ms on the Jetson.

  • 43.22%four-class accuracy, chance is 25%
  • +4.56 ptsover EEGNet on unseen subjects
  • 0 trialsof labeled calibration per user
  • 0.75 msinference on Jetson Orin Nano
Published, IEEE R10-HTC 2023

Leveraging Gram Matrix Representation in Shallow DNN for GI Tract MRI Image Segmentation

Fariza Siddiqua, Tamim Ahmed, Mohammed Imamul Hassan Bhuiyan

Before radiation treatment of GI tract tumors, oncologists must outline the stomach and bowels on MRI so the beam avoids them, which takes 15 minutes to hours by hand. U-Net-family models automate this but are heavy. My undergraduate thesis replaced the attention mechanism with Gram-matrix features so a much shallower network could do the job.

Approach

A U-shaped network whose five encoder stages are GCFM (Gram matrix concatenated feature matrix) blocks. Each block turns its feature maps into vectors, computes a Gram matrix of their correlations, and concatenates it with the original features, telling the network which features matter. That allows smaller filters and fewer layers, with mostly concatenation instead of multiplication.

Result

On the UW-Madison GI tract MRI dataset (stomach, large bowel and small bowel), the model reached the highest IoU of the five models compared, 0.912, with Dice and loss on par with U-Net and U-Net++. It does this with 9.3 million parameters, about 75% fewer than U-Net.

  • 0.912 IoUhighest of five models
  • 0.901 Diceon par with U-Net and U-Net++
  • 75% fewerparameters than U-Net
  • +25% IoUover LeViT-U-Net++
